sentences.text: Igdamanosaurus was a small reptile belonging to the family Mosasauridae.
It is recognized by its rounded, knob-like teeth, which were straight, broad cones with rounded, domed tips and a subcircular cross-section.
Each tooth had an unwaisted base covered in approximately 65 to 70 fine parallel ridges, with the largest preserved specimen measuring approximately 27 mm in height and 22 mm in width.
The animal possessed a dentary of massive proportions similar to those of Globidens and Prognathodon.
Despite its small size, comparable to its relative Carinodens, this mosasaur used its teeth to crush armored prey such as molluscs and turtles instead of typical fish or reptile prey.
The specialized nature of these teeth suggests it had a durophagous diet, likely crushing hard-shelled prey.
The genus Igdamanosaurus was named by Lingham-Soliar in 1991, though the species was originally named Globidens aegyptiacus by Zdansky in 1935 before being moved to its own genus.
Fossils of this animal have been found in the Duwi Formation of Egypt and the Dukamaje Formation of Niger.
Igdamanosaurus used its teeth to crush armored prey such as molluscs and turtles instead of typical fish or reptile prey.

Recent analyses place Igdamanosaurus within the Mosasaurinae tribe Globidensini as a relative of Carinodens and Globidens, classifying it as a member of the subfamily Mosasaurinae and the family Mosasauridae.
Lingham-Soliar (1991) initially classified Igdamanosaurus within the Plioplatecarpinae based on vertical striae suggesting a Platecarpus-like ancestor.
Igdamanosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage, in marine environments in Africa between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
